property_summary: After calling Put(value, unlockTime) by any sender with any value, the contract C always sets the caller's Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime to at least the current block.timestamp (i.e. max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp)); the mutant that assigns acc.unlockTime = _unlockTime can set it below block.timestamp for some fuzzed _unlockTime, violating this invariant.

For every call to Put by any sender with any value, the reference contract ensures Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime >= block.timestamp (it clamps _unlockTime up to now); the mutant that assigns acc.unlockTime = _unlockTime can produce unlockTime < block.timestamp for some fuzzed _unlockTime, violating this property.

For any Put(...) call by any sender, the reference C ensures that after the call the holder's unlockTime is at least the timestamp when Put executed (it never sets unlockTime in the past); the mutant that assigns acc.unlockTime = _unlockTime can set unlockTime < block.timestamp for some fuzzed _unlockTime and thus violate this invariant.

For any Put call, if the caller provides an _unlockTime that is >= block.timestamp then the reference will set Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime equal to that provided value (it preserves future unlock times), whereas the mutant may set a lower value when given a past unlockTime — so we assert that when _unlockTime >= block.timestamp, the stored unlockTime equals _unlockTime.

For any Put call, if the caller supplies _unlockTime less than or equal to block.timestamp then the reference C will store Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime equal to block.timestamp (it clamps past times up to now); the mutant that assigns acc.unlockTime = _unlockTime can leave a past unlockTime and thus make Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime < block.timestamp.

For any caller and any payment, calling Put(_unlockTime) sets the caller's recorded unlockTime to max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp) (allowing extending the lock into the future); the mutant instead always sets unlockTime to block.timestamp and thus can never set a future unlock time.

For any caller and any provided _unlockTime, after calling Put with a positive msg.value the contract's stored unlockTime for that caller is >= block.timestamp and equals max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp); the mutant that always sets unlockTime = block.timestamp can be shown to produce a stored unlockTime < provided future _unlockTime when the fuzzer supplies a future _unlockTime > block.timestamp.

For any caller and any supplied _unlockTime and positive payment, after Put the stored unlockTime for that caller is at least block.timestamp and equals max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp); the mutant that forces unlockTime=block.timestamp will violate equality when _unlockTime > block.timestamp.

For any caller, any positive deposit amount, and any supplied _unlockTime, after calling Put the stored Acc[caller].unlockTime equals the greater of the supplied _unlockTime and the current block.timestamp; the mutant that always sets unlockTime = block.timestamp violates this when the fuzzer supplies a future _unlockTime > block.timestamp.

For any caller and any provided _unlockTime and deposit, calling Put stores Acc[caller].unlockTime = max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp); the mutant that always sets unlockTime = block.timestamp will violate this whenever the fuzzer supplies a future _unlockTime (> block.timestamp).

For any caller and any payable amount, calling Put increases that caller's recorded Acc.balance by exactly the sent msg.value on top of the previous balance (i.e., Acc.balance_new == Acc.balance_old + msg.value); the mutant overwrites balance with msg.value and thus can violate this accumulation when a caller deposits twice or when previous balance > 0.

For every caller and every sequence of two deposits, the contract's recorded balance after the second deposit equals the sum of the prior recorded balance and the second deposit (i.e., balances accumulate: Acc[addr].balance_new == Acc[addr].balance_old + msg.value); the mutant overwrites the balance with msg.value and thus can violate accumulation when prior balance > 0.

For any caller and any deposit amount, after calling Put the contract's recorded Acc[caller].balance is at least as large as the single most recent deposit (i.e., Acc[caller].balance >= last msg.value); the mutant that overwrites balance with msg.value can violate this when prior balance > last msg.value, making Acc balance < previous accumulation and still equal to only msg.value.

For every caller and any deposit amount, calling Put increases that caller's recorded Acc.balance to be >= the previous Acc.balance (i.e., Put never decreases an account's stored balance); the mutant that overwrites acc.balance = msg.value can decrease balance when prior balance > msg.value, breaking this rule.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, calling Put never reduces that depositor's recorded Acc.balance (i.e., Acc[addr].balance_after >= Acc[addr].balance_before); the mutant that sets acc.balance = msg.value can decrease the stored balance when prior balance > msg.value, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any ether value >= 0, calling Put(...) on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) and increases the caller's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance by exactly msg.value; the mutant that requires msg.value > 0 will revert (or fail to update balance) for zero-value deposits, breaking this rule for inputs with msg.value == 0.

For any caller and any ether value >= 0, calling Put(...) always succeeds and increments Acc[caller].balance by exactly msg.value; the mutant that requires msg.value > 0 breaks this by reverting (or not allowing) zero-value deposits, so there exist inputs with msg.value == 0 where the mutant violates the property.

For any caller and any ether value, calling Put(...) never reverts and after the call the contract's Acc[caller].balance increases by exactly msg.value; the mutant that requires msg.value > 0 will revert for msg.value == 0 and thus violate this rule.

For any caller and any uint unlockTime and any ether value > = 0, calling Put(unlockTime) on the reference never reverts (succeeds); the mutant that adds require(msg.value > 0) will revert when msg.value == 0, so there exist inputs (zero-value deposit) that make the mutant revert while the reference allows it.

For all callers and any unlockTime and ether value, calling Put(unlockTime) on the reference never reverts and after the call Acc[caller].balance increases by msg.value (including when msg.value == 0); the mutant that adds require(msg.value > 0) will revert for msg.value == 0, thus violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero msg.value, calling Put(...) on the reference always records the deposit by increasing the caller's Acc balance (and logs it), whereas the mutant returns early on msg.value == 0 which only affects zero-value calls — therefore the general rule: after Put is called with value v, Acc[caller].balance increases by v; the mutant violates this when v==0 because it returns without updating or logging.

For any caller and any sent value v, after calling Put(v) the caller's Acc balance increases by exactly v (i.e., Acc[caller].balance == previous + v); the mutant returns early when v==0 and thus can violate this rule for v==0.

For any caller and any sent value v, calling Put(...) increases Acc[caller].balance by v (including when v == 0); the mutant returns early on msg.value == 0 and thus can violate this by leaving balance unchanged for zero-value calls.

For any caller and any sent msg.value, calling Put(_unlockTime) leaves Acc[caller].balance equal to its previous value plus msg.value (including when msg.value == 0); the mutant returns early when msg.value == 0 and thus can violate this by not updating the balance for zero-value calls.

For any caller and any sent value v, after calling Put(_unlockTime) the caller's Acc balance equals its previous balance plus v (including v == 0); the mutant returns early when v == 0 and thus can violate this rule for zero-value calls.

For any caller who has deposited at least MinSum, calling Collect(x) that succeeds in sending x must always reduce the caller's recorded balance by x; the mutant that moves the balance update after the external call can fail to reduce the stored balance when the callee's receive/call reverts, so the invariant is broken for some inputs (a failing external counterparty).

For any caller and any amount, if Collect(...) returns (does not revert) after a call that transfers funds out, then the contract's stored Acc[caller].balance is decreased by that amount; the mutant that moves the balance update after the external call can return successfully yet leave Acc[caller].balance unchanged when the external transfer to a failing/reverting counterparty behaves adversarially.

For any caller that has deposited at least MinSum, if Collect(...) returns successfully then the caller's stored Acc[caller].balance is always decreased by the collected amount; the mutant that moves the state update after the external call can return successfully while leaving the recorded balance unchanged when the external transfer reverts or fails.

If Collect(...) returns successfully for a caller, then that caller's recorded Acc[caller].balance is decreased by the withdrawn amount; the mutant that moves the balance update after the external call can return successfully while leaving Acc[caller].balance unchanged when the external transfer to a reverting callee behaves adversarially.

For any caller and amount, whenever Collect(...) returns successfully the caller's stored Acc[caller].balance decreases by the collected amount; the mutant that moves the balance update to after the external call can return successfully while leaving the stored balance unchanged when the external transfer to a reverting callee fails, violating this invariant.

For every input, the reference contract C only allows Collect to succeed when block.timestamp > acc.unlockTime (i.e., collection is disallowed at exactly unlockTime); the mutant using >= lets a withdrawal succeed at block.timestamp == unlockTime for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For any caller and amounts, the reference C never allows Collect to succeed when block.timestamp == acc.unlockTime (requires strictly >), while the mutant with >= can succeed at that exact timestamp for some inputs.

For all admissible inputs, the reference contract C never allows Collect to succeed when block.timestamp == acc.unlockTime (collection requires strictly >); the mutant changes the check to >= allowing Collect to succeed at the exact unlockTime for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any depositor and amount, the reference contract C never allows Collect(...) to transfer funds when block.timestamp == acc.unlockTime (it requires block.timestamp > acc.unlockTime); the mutant using >= can succeed at that exact timestamp for some inputs, so the property is that Collect must fail at timestamp == unlockTime.

For every caller and amounts, the reference contract C never allows Collect(...) to succeed when block.timestamp == acc.unlockTime (requires strictly >); the mutant changes the check to >= which allows success at that exact timestamp for some inputs.
